claim: Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS) were introduced to assess the formation of Pou5f3 complexes with other transcription factors in real-time in gastrulating zebrafish embryos.
source: Here, we introduce fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy and fluorescence correlation spectroscopy to assess the formation of Pou5f3 complexes with other transcription factors in real-time in gastrulating zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Pou5f3 complexes with Nanog to pattern mesendoderm differentiation at the blastula stage at single-cell resolution in vivo.
source: We show, at single-cell resolution in vivo, that Pou5f3 complexes with Nanog to pattern mesendoderm differentiation at the blastula stage.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FLIM-FRET and FCCS data presented in the results.

claim: During gastrulation, Sox32 restricts Pou5f3–Nanog complexes to the ventrolateral mesendoderm by binding Pou5f3 or Nanog in prospective dorsal endoderm.
source: Later, during gastrulation, Sox32 restricts Pou5f3–Nanog complexes to the ventrolateral mesendoderm by binding Pou5f3 or Nanog in prospective dorsal endoderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by FLIM-FRET data showing Sox32 interactions with Pou5f3 and Nanog.

claim: In the ventrolateral endoderm, the Elabela/Aplnr pathway limits Sox32 levels, allowing the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes and the activation of downstream BMP signaling.
source: In the ventrolateral endoderm, the Elabela / Aplnr pathway limits Sox32 levels, allowing the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes and the activation of downstream BMP signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data from elabr13 mutant embryos showing altered Sox32 levels and Pou5f3-Nanog complex formation.

claim: A balance in the spatiotemporal distribution of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes, modulated by Sox32, regulates mesendoderm specification along the dorsoventral axis.
source: This quantitative model shows that a balance in the spatiotemporal distribution of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes, modulated by Sox32, regulates mesendoderm specification along the dorsoventral axis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings from FLIM, FCS, and genetic experiments.

claim: Oct4 drives cell lineage commitment in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Previous studies have suggested that Oct4 drives cell lineage commitment in a dose-dependent manner (Niwa et al., 2000; Thomson et al., 2011), switching gene regulatory regions (Aksoy et al., 2013) by diffusive behaviors (Kaur et al., 2013; Plachta et al., 2011) and mediating changes in chromatin structure (Abboud et al., 2015; Carey et al., 2014; Hogan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mammalian Pou5f1/Oct4 can functionally replace its paralogue Pou5f3 in zebrafish embryos.
source: Mammalian Pou5f1/Oct4 can functionally replace its paralogue Pou5f3 (Frankenberg et al., 2014) in zebrafish embryos, with evidence showing that overexpressed Oct4 can rescue the phenotype of maternal-zygotic (MZ) spg embryos that lack Pou5f3 function (Onichtchouk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Maternal Pou5f3 regulates dorsoventral (DV) patterning.
source: Maternal Pou5f3 regulates dorsoventral (DV) patterning (Belting et al., 2011; Reim and Brand, 2006) and endoderm formation (Lunde et al., 2004; Reim et al., 2004), whereas the establishment of the mid–hindbrain boundary requires zygotic expression of Pou5f3 (Belting et al., 2001; Reim and Brand, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pou5f3 induces mesendoderm ventralization through activation of the BMP pathway and the expression of the Vent family of TFs.
source: Pou5f3 induces mesendoderm ventralization through activation of the BMP pathway and the expression of the Vent (Vent, Ved and Vox) family of TFs (Reim and Brand, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Nanog is critical for endoderm induction through the Mxtx-Nodal pathway where it induces sox32 in mesendodermal cells.
source: In contrast, Nanog is critical for endoderm induction through the Mxtx-Nodal pathway where it induces sox32 in mesendodermal cells and other early, endoderm regulators, such as gata5, mixer, nrd1 and nrd2 (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The GFP-Oct4 fusion protein was able to complement the spg phenotype in 30% of injected embryos.
source: The GFP-Oct4 fusion protein was able to complement the spg phenotype in 30% of injected embryos.
evidence: This is a direct experimental result from the phenotype complementation assay.

claim: At the blastula stage (oblong stage; 3.5 hpf), the GFP-Oct4 concentration was 44.39 ± 1.54 nM.
source: At the blastula stage (oblong stage; 3.5 hpf), the GFP-Oct4 concentration was 44.39 ± 1.54 nM (Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement obtained from FCS experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Non-rescued embryos arrested at the oblong stage had similar Oct4 concentrations (43.90 ± 18.30 nM) to those of rescued embryos.
source: Non-rescued embryos arrested at the oblong stage (Figure 1b) had similar Oct4 concentrations (43.90 ± 18.30 nM) to those of rescued embryos (Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FCS measurements shown in Figure 1.

claim: The DNA-bound fraction (F2) was significantly lower in the non-rescued embryos (0.19 ± 0.08) as compared with the rescued ones (0.27 ± 0.01) (p<0.0001).
source: However, the DNA-bound fraction (F2) was significantly lower in the non-rescued embryos (0.19 ± 0.08) as compared with the rescued ones (0.27 ± 0.01) (p<0.0001; Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FCS measurements with statistical significance shown in Figure 1.

claim: When a construct of Oct4 lacking its homeodomain (GFP-Oct4ΔHD) was used, the DNA-bound fraction further decreased to 0.12 ± 0.01, and all embryos arrested at the oblong stage.
source: When a construct of Oct4 lacking its homeodomain (GFP-Oct4ΔHD) was used instead, the DNA-bound fraction further decreased, and all embryos arrested at the oblong stage (0.12 ± 0.01) (p<0.0001; Figure 1c–e and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental result from FCS measurements using a deletion construct shown in Figure 1.

claim: Specific levels of the Oct4 DNA-bound active fraction are crucial for proper embryo gastrulation.
source: These results suggest that specific levels of the Oct4 DNA-bound active fraction—and, by extension, Pou5f3—are crucial for proper embryo gastrulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FCS data showing correlation between DNA-bound fraction and developmental progression.

claim: Mesendodermal cells showed a significantly higher proportion of the DNA-bound active fraction of GFP-Oct4 protein as compared with ectodermal cells (0.27 ± 0.01 vs 0.19 ± 0.01, respectively; p<0.0001).
source: Mesendodermal cells showed a significantly higher proportion of the DNA-bound active fraction of GFP-Oct4 protein as compared with ectodermal cells (0.27 ± 0.01 vs 0.19 ± 0.01, respectively; p<0.0001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FCS measurements in different cell lineages shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the oblong stage, the DNA-bound active fraction of Oct4 was higher in the mesendoderm than in the ectoderm lineage.
source: Thus, at the oblong stage, the DNA-bound active fraction of Oct4 was higher in the mesendoderm than in the ectoderm lineage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the FCS measurements comparing mesendoderm and ectoderm.

claim: Co-injection of low dose nanog MO with GFP-Oct4 mRNA led to a reduction in the bound fraction of GFP-Oct4 from 0.27 ± 0.01 to 0.22 ± 0.01 (p<0.001) in mesendoderm.
source: This co-injection led to a reduction in the bound fraction of GFP-Oct4 from 0.27 ± 0.01 to 0.22 ± 0.01 (p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FCS measurements in nanog morphants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The GFP-Nanog DNA-bound active fraction in pou5f3 morphants was reduced from 0.21 ± 0.01 to 0.16 ± 0.01 (p<0.001).
source: As a control, we carried out the reverse experiment to assess the GFP-Nanog DNA-bound active fraction in pou5f3 morphants, measuring a reduction from 0.21 ± 0.01 to 0.16 ± 0.01 (p<0.001; Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FCS measurements in pou5f3 morphants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Pou5f3- and Nanog-binding fractions are dependent on each other in mesendoderm lineage.
source: These FCS data suggest that the Pou5f3- and Nanog-binding fractions are dependent on each other in mesendoderm lineage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reciprocal knockdown experiments showing mutual dependence.

claim: A Kd of 15.34 ± 1.6 nM was measured for Oct4-Nanog interaction in the mesendoderm and 61.9 ± 7.5 nM in the ectoderm, suggesting higher binding affinity in mesendoderm at the oblong stage.
source: We measured a Kd of 15.34 ± 1.6 nM and 61.9 ± 7.5 nM in the mesendoderm and ectoderm, respectively, suggesting higher binding affinity in mesendoderm at the oblong stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FCCS experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: A significant reduction in the GFP-Oct4 lifetime was found in the presence of mCherry-Nanog in the mesendoderm (1.79 ± 0.05 ns; p<0.0001) but not in the ectoderm (2.28 ± 0.01 ns) as compared with the GFP-Oct4 lifetime in the absence of mCherry-Nanog (2.30 ± 0.01 ns).
source: In the nuclei of individual cells within the mesendoderm and ectoderm of oblong stage embryos (3.5 hpf; Figure 2d), we found a significant reduction in the GFP-Oct4 lifetime in the presence of mCherry-Nanog in the mesendoderm (1.79 ± 0.05 ns; p<0.0001) but not in the ectoderm (2.28 ± 0.01 ns; Figure 2d) as compared with the GFP-Oct4 lifetime in the absence of mCherry-Nanog (2.30 ± 0.01 ns; Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FLIM-FRET experiments shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The binding percentages of Oct4-Nanog in the mesendoderm and ectoderm were 27% and 2.2%, respectively.
source: the binding percentages (Orthaus et al., 2009) in the mesendoderm and ectoderm were 27% and 2.2%, respectively (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation from FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: FLIM-FRET results demonstrate a higher proportion of Oct4–Nanog complexes in the mesendoderm as compared with that in ectoderm at the oblong stage.
source: These FLIM-FRET results demonstrate a higher proportion of Oct4–Nanog complexes in the mesendoderm as compared with that in ectoderm at the oblong stage and suggest that Pou5f3 and Nanog co-regulate mesendoderm targets during gastrulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FLIM-FRET measurements comparing mesendoderm and ectoderm.

claim: At 50% epiboly, the Kd values in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm (5.4 ± 0.4 nM and 11.1 ± 0.73 nM, respectively) indicated a high-binding affinity as compared with that in the dorsal mesendoderm (36.8 ± 3.5 nM).
source: In contrast, the Kd values in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm (5.4 ± 0.4 nM and 11.1 ± 0.73 nM, respectively) indicated a high-binding affinity in these regions as compared with that in the dorsal mesendoderm (36.8 ± 3.5 nM) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FCCS experiments at different spatial locations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The GFP-Oct4 lifetime was significantly reduced in the presence of mCherry-Nanog in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm (2.29 ± 0.01 ns to 2.02 ± 0.01 ns and 2.03 ± 0.02 ns, respectively; p<0.0001) but not in dorsal mesendoderm (2.31 ± 0.01 ns).
source: We found that the GFP-Oct4 lifetime was significantly reduced in the presence of mCherry-Nanog in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm (2.29 ± 0.01 ns in absence of mCherry-Nanog to 2.02 ± 0.01 ns and 2.03 ± 0.02 ns, respectively; p<0.0001; Figure 3b) but not in dorsal mesendoderm (2.31 ± 0.01 ns; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FLIM-FRET experiments at different spatial locations shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The percentage of Oct4-Nanog binding was greater than 20% in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm but only 4.7% in the dorsal area.
source: The percentage of binding was greater than 20% in the ventral and lateral mesendoderm but only 4.7% in the dorsal area (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a quantitative calculation from FLIM-FRET data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Cells from radial dorsal structures in LiCl-treated embryos showed a similar percentage of Oct4–Nanog binding to that of cells from the dorsal mesendoderm of non-treated embryos (2% and 4.7%, respectively).
source: The cells from these radial dorsal structures showed a similar percentage of Oct4–Nanog binding to that of cells from the dorsal mesendoderm of non-treated embryos (2% and 4.7%, respectively; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FLIM-FRET experiments in dorsalized embryos shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Uneven yet specific levels of the Pou5f3–Nanog complex may drive DV mesendodermal patterning.
source: These results suggest that uneven yet specific levels of the Pou5f3–Nanog complex may drive DV mesendodermal patterning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial distribution data of Pou5f3-Nanog complexes.

claim: With 1.6 ng of nanog MO, 90% of morphants were Class IV (poorly developed axial structures, and no apparent eyes, trunk or tail).
source: With 1.6 ng of nanog MO, we observed that 90% of morphants were Class (C) IV (poorly developed axial structures, and no apparent eyes, trunk or tail) (Figure 4a,b)
evidence: This is a phenotypic observation from nanog knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: With 0.4 ng of nanog MO, 70% of morphants showed C III (truncated bodies and hypoplastic eyes) and C II phenotypes (normal head structures, a short body axis, a bent tail and no fins).
source: with 0.4 ng of nanog MO, 70% of morphants showed C III (truncated bodies and hypoplastic eyes) and C II phenotypes (normal head structures, a short body axis, a bent tail and no fins) (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is a phenotypic observation from nanog knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Near complete rescue (C I) was observed when 0.1 ng of nanog mRNA (lacking the MO-target site) was co-injected with 0.4 ng of MO.
source: Near complete rescue (C I) was observed when 0.1 ng of nanog mRNA (lacking the MO-target site) was co-injected with 0.4 ng of MO (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This is a rescue experiment result shown in Figure 4.

claim: In nanog morphants at 30% epiboly, chd was expressed circumferentially, and at 50% epiboly, chd transcripts were ubiquitous.
source: In particular, the expression of chd at the dorsal pole was up-regulated dramatically: at the 30% epiboly stage, chd was expressed circumferentially, whereas at 50% epiboly, chd transcripts were ubiquitous (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in nanog morphants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: nanog morphants showed significantly down-regulated bmp4 and bmp2b expression.
source: Whereas bmp2b expression was localized at the embryonic shield and broadly expressed ventrally at the 70% epiboly stage in controls, nanog morphants showed significantly down-regulated bmp4 (data not shown) and bmp2b expression (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in nanog morphants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The expression of direct targets of BMP signaling, such as vox and vent, was greatly reduced in nanog morphants at the 50% epiboly stage.
source: Consistently, the expression of direct targets of BMP signaling, such as vox and vent, was greatly reduced in nanog morphants at the 50% epiboly stage (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in nanog morphants shown in Figure 4c.

claim: nanog knockdown leads to the dorsalization of embryos and maternal nanog activity is necessary for ventral cell specification by BMPs.
source: Together, these results indicate that nanog knockdown leads to the dorsalization of embryos and that maternal nanog activity is necessary for ventral cell specification by BMPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the gene expression and phenotypic analyses of nanog morphants.

claim: Expansion of the dorsal marker, chd, was more pronounced in MZspg/nanog-deficient embryos as compared with nanog morphants or MZspg mutants at the 50% epiboly stage.
source: Expansion of the dorsal marker, chd, was more pronounced in MZspg/nanog-deficient embryos as compared with nanog morphants or MZspg mutants at the 50% epiboly stage (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in double mutants shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The ventral marker, vox, was absent in MZspg/nanog-deficient embryos but only reduced in both nanog morphants and MZspg mutants.
source: Conversely, the ventral marker, vox, was absent in MZspg/nanog-deficient embryos but only reduced in both nanog morphants and MZspg mutants (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in double mutants shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Injection of nanog mRNA into MZspg mutants failed to rescue the expression of chd.
source: Injection of nanog mRNA into MZspg mutants failed to rescue the expression of chd (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a rescue experiment result shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Injection of pou5f3 mRNA into nanog morphants could not rescue DV patterning.
source: Similarly, injection of pou5f3 mRNA into nanog morphants could not rescue DV patterning (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is a rescue experiment result shown in Figure 4e.

claim: pou5f3 and nanog display overlapping functions during DV patterning but cannot compensate for one another.
source: These results suggest that pou5f3 and nanog display overlapping functions during DV patterning but cannot compensate for one another.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the rescue experiments showing lack of mutual compensation.

claim: Nanog must cooperate with Pou5f3 to promote ventral fate.
source: This is consistent with the notion that Nanog must cooperate with Pou5f3 to promote ventral fate.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the genetic interaction experiments.

claim: In sox32 morphants, a significant reduction in the lifetime of GFP-Oct4 in the presence of mCherry-Nanog was observed (2.31 ± 0.01 ns to 2.16 ± 0.03 ns, p<0.0001), and an increase in the binding percentage from 1% to 15% in the dorsal endoderm precursors at 50% epiboly.
source: In sox32 morphants, we saw a significant reduction in the lifetime of GFP-Oct4 in the presence of mCherry-Nanog (2.31 ± 0.01 ns to 2.16 ± 0.03 ns, p<0.0001; Figure 5a-c), and an increase in the binding percentage from 1% to 15%, indicating that the Oct4–Nanog complex forms in the absence of Sox32 in the dorsal endoderm precursors at 50% epiboly (Figure 5a-c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FLIM-FRET experiments in sox32 morphants shown in Figure 5.

claim: The GFP-Sox32 lifetime was significantly reduced from 2.54 ± 0.01 ns in the absence of mCherry-Oct4 to 2.21 ± 0.04 ns in presence of mCherry-Oct4, with a binding percentage of 18% (p<0.0001).
source: We found that the GFP-Sox32 lifetime was significantly reduced from 2.54 ± 0.01 ns in the absence of mCherry-Oct4 to 2.21 ± 0.04 ns in presence of mCherry-Oct4, with a binding percentage of 18% (p<0.0001; Figure 5a-c).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FLIM-FRET experiments showing Sox32-Oct4 interaction shown in Figure 5.

claim: Nanog also interacts with Sox32 in the dorsal endoderm at 50% epiboly.
source: Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Figure 5—source data 1 show that Nanog also interacts with Sox32 in the dorsal endoderm at 50% epiboly.
evidence: This is stated with reference to supplementary figure data showing Nanog-Sox32 interaction.

claim: Sox32 prevents the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes at the 50% epiboly stage in dorsal aspects and restricts them to the ventrolateral mesendoderm.
source: Together, these results suggest that Sox32 prevents the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes at the 50% epiboly stage in dorsal aspects and restricts them to the ventrolateral mesendoderm.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FLIM-FRET experiments in sox32 morphants and wild-type embryos.

claim: A significant reduction in GFP-Oct4 lifetime was observed in the presence of mCherry-Nanog in ventrolateral mesoderm and endoderm at 60% epiboly (from 2.31 ± 0.01 ns to 2.01 ± 0.02 ns and 1.98 ± 0.02 ns, respectively; p<0.0001).
source: We observed a significant reduction in GFP-Oct4 lifetime from 2.31 ± 0.01 ns to 2.01 ± 0.02 ns and 1.98 ± 0.02 ns in the ventrolateral mesoderm and endoderm, respectively (p<0.0001; (Figure 6a–c)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from FLIM-FRET experiments at 60% epiboly shown in Figure 6.

claim: Pou5f3–Nanog complexes may be involved in ventrolateral patterning at later stages.
source: suggesting that Pou5f3–Nanog complexes may be involved in ventrolateral patterning at later stages.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FLIM-FRET data at 60% epiboly.

claim: sox32 levels are higher in elabr13 embryos than in control siblings (p<0.01).
source: Likewise, sox32 levels are higher in elabr13 embryos than in control siblings (p<0.01; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In elabr13 embryos, the percentage of Oct4–Nanog complexes in endodermal cells was significantly reduced from 21% to 15% (p<0.01).
source: Interestingly, in contrast to mesodermal cells, the percentage of Oct4–Nanog complexes in endodermal cells was significantly reduced from 21% to 15% (p<0.01; Figure 6e).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison from FLIM-FRET experiments in elabr13 mutants shown in Figure 6e.

claim: Sox32 regulates Pou5f3–Nanog complexes by protein competition and modulates endoderm formation in a spatiotemporal manner along the DV axis.
source: Thus, these results support the idea that Sox32 regulates Pou5f3–Nanog complexes by protein competition and, thus, modulates endoderm formation in a spatiotemporal manner along the DV axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experiments in elabr13 mutants showing altered Sox32 levels and Pou5f3-Nanog complex formation.

claim: bmp4 expression was more reduced and restricted to the ventral area of elabr13 embryos.
source: We found that bmp4 expression was more reduced and restricted to the ventral area of elabr13 embryos.
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from in situ hybridization in elabr13 mutants.

claim: bmp2b and bmp2a expression was lower in elabr13 embryos as compared to wt embryos.
source: bmp2b and bmp2a expression was also lower in elabr13 embryos as compared to wt embryos (Figure 6f).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from qRT-PCR shown in Figure 6f.

claim: her5, which is expressed in a dorsal subpopulation of endodermal precursors, was significantly increased in elabr13 embryos.
source: whereas her5, which is expressed in a dorsal subpopulation of endodermal precursors (Müller et al., 1996b), was significantly increased (Figure 6f–g).
evidence: This is a gene expression observation from qRT-PCR and in situ hybridization in elabr13 mutants shown in Figure 6f-g.

claim: The Elabela/Aplnr pathway, by controlling sox32 levels, quantitatively modulates Oct4-Nanog complex formation to refine BMP signaling during DV patterning of the endoderm.
source: Thus, our data show that the Elabela / Aplnr pathway, by controlling sox32 levels, quantitatively modulates Oct4-Nanog complex formation to refine BMP signaling during DV patterning of the endoderm.
evidence: This is a conclusion synthesizing the findings from elabr13 mutant analysis.

claim: The rescue of maternal spg function depends on Oct4 DNA-binding.
source: Our FCS experiments show that the rescue of maternal spg function depends on Oct4 DNA-binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FCS experiments showing correlation between DNA-bound fraction and rescue.

claim: A switch in the partners of Pou5f3 must play a role in cell fate determination.
source: Our results, showing a lineage dependency on such an Oct4–DNA interaction, support the view that a switch in the partners of Pou5f3 must play a role in cell fate determination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the lineage-specific differences in Oct4 DNA-binding and complex formation.

claim: Pou5f3 and Nanog may act together to control zygotic genes in mesendoderm and thereby limit lineage commitment in pluripotent cells.
source: Given that Sox proteins in mesendoderm do not co-regulatePou5f3 targets (Onichtchouk et al., 2010), we speculate that Pou5f3 and Nanog may act together to control zygotic genes in mesendoderm and thereby limit lineage commitment in pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed Pou5f3-Nanog complexes in mesendoderm and cited literature.

claim: During the transition from blastula to gastrula, dorsal factors may compete with Nanog to partner with Pou5f3, which in turn, may restrict the expression of BMP ligands to the ventral aspects of the embryo.
source: The presence of Oct4–Nanog complexes at the ventrolateral but not dorsal mesendoderm suggests that, during the transition from blastula to gastrula, dorsal factors may compete with Nanog to partner with Pou5f3, which in turn, may restrict the expression of BMP ligands to the ventral aspects of the embryo.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the spatial distribution of Pou5f3-Nanog complexes and BMP expression patterns.

claim: Sox32 prevents the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes in dorsal endoderm precursors by binding either with Pou5f3 or Nanog.
source: Oct4–Nanog complexes are detectable following the knock down of sox32, indicating that Sox32, which interacts in vivo with Oct4 in these cells, competes with Nanog for Oct4 binding. We also found that Nanog complexes with Sox32 in the same group of cells, suggesting that Sox32 prevents the formation of Pou5f3–Nanog complexes in dorsal endoderm precursors by binding either with Pou5f3 or Nanog.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion from the FLIM-FRET experiments showing Sox32 interactions with both Pou5f3 and Nanog.

claim: Nanog, in addition to its role with Pou5f3 upstream of BMP signaling and in regulating ventrolateral endoderm through the Nodal pathway, may have other roles in patterning the DV axis in zebrafish.
source: The presence of the Sox32–Nanog complex suggests that Nanog, in addition to its role with Pou5f3 upstream of BMP signaling and in regulating ventrolateral endoderm through the Nodal pathway (Xu et al., 2012), may have other roles in patterning the DV axis in zebrafish.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed Sox32-Nanog complexes.

claim: Oct4–Nanog, Sox32–Oct4 and Sox32–Nanog complexes coexist in ventrolateral endodermal cells during gastrulation.
source: We also provide evidence that Oct4–Nanog, Sox32–Oct4 and Sox32–Nanog complexes coexist in ventrolateral endodermal cells during gastrulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the FLIM-FRET and FCCS experiments showing multiple protein interactions.

claim: The Elabela/Aplnr pathway is essential for proper endoderm differentiation, as it regulates the proliferation and migration of the endoderm precursors.
source: The Elabela / Aplnr pathway is essential for proper endoderm differentiation, as it regulates the proliferation and migration of the endoderm precursors (www.elabela.com; Chng et al., 2013; Pauli et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: When the Ela pathway is inhibited, the levels of sox32 increase, accompanied by a decrease in the percentage of Oct4–Nanog complexes in endodermal cells.
source: Interestingly, when the Ela pathway is inhibited, the levels of sox32 increase, accompanied by a decrease in the percentage of Oct4–Nanog complexes in endodermal cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from elabr13 mutant analysis.

claim: her5 is known to control the anteroposterior migration of endodermal progenitors, a process that is acutely affected in Ela-null embryos.
source: her5, in particular, is known to control the anteroposterior migration of endodermal progenitors (Tiso et al., 2002), a process that is acutely affected in Ela-null embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study and connects to the observed phenotype.

claim: FCS has been previously used to study dynamic processes, such as blood flow or morphogen gradients in living zebrafish embryos.
source: FCS (Figure 1a) has been previously used to study dynamic processes, such as blood flow (Pan et al., 2007) or morphogen gradients (Yu et al., 2009) in living zebrafish embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Recent studies have described the use of FCS to analyze TF protein activity in iPScells and pre-gastrula mouse embryos.
source: Recent studies have described the use of FCS to analyze TF protein activity in iPScells (Lam et al., 2012) and pre-gastrula mouse embryos (Kaur et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In zebrafish, unlike in mammals, it is possible to follow mesendoderm and ectoderm formation during early development.
source: In zebrafish, unlike in mammals, it is possible to follow mesendoderm and ectoderm formation during early development (Fong et al., 2005) (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: 83.7% of dextran red-negative cells are mesendodermal when dextran red is injected into two central cells at the 16-cell stage.
source: For that purpose, zygotes were injected with GFP-Oct4 mRNA followed by dextran red as a lineage tracer into two central cells at the 16-cell stage, such that the dextran red-positive cells are entirely ectodermal, whereas 83.7% of the negative cells are mesendodermal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the lineage tracing approach.

claim: Oct4 and Nanog share many genomic binding sites.
source: Since Oct4 and Nanog share many genomic binding sites (Loh et al., 2006; van den Berg et al., 2010), we next investigated whether they interact in vivo in a cell lineage-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: We have previously shown that Oct4 interacts with Sox2 in ESCs and iPSCs using FLIM-FRET.
source: We have previously shown that Oct4 interacts with Sox2 in ESCs and iPSCs using this method (Lam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Dorsal endodermal precursors arise from cells in the dorsal mesendoderm near the margin before the cells involute to form the hipoblast.
source: Lineage tracing experiments have shown that dorsal endodermal precursors arise from cells in the dorsal mesendoderm near the margin before the cells involute to form the hipoblast, and that those situated above are restricted to the mesoderm (Warga and Nüsslein-Volhard, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sox32 expression starts in the dorsal endodermal cells at 4 hpf and extends to ventrolateral endoderm.
source: Previously, we have shown that Oct4 and Nanog form complexes in the whole mesendoderm at 3.5 hpf and, by 4 hpf, Sox32 expression starts in the dorsal endodermal cells and extends to ventrolateral endoderm (Thisse et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Elabela mutant (elabr13) embryos have a significantly lower number of endodermal progenitors that express sox17.
source: Elabela mutant (elabr13) embryos have a significantly lower number of endodermal progenitors that express sox17; yet, the total levels of sox17 are still higher in elabr13 embryos than in control siblings (Chng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: BMP signaling is initially uniform at the blastula stage and is shaped by inhibitors from the dorsal side at the beginning of gastrulation.
source: BMP signaling is initially uniform at the blastula stage and is shaped by inhibitors from the dorsal side at the beginning of gastrulation (Blader et al., 1997; Kishimoto et al., 1997; Reversade and De Robertis, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromatin modifications can influence long- and short-lived TF DNA binding in early mouse embryos.
source: In particular, chromatin modifications can influence long- and short-lived TF DNA binding in early mouse embryos (White et al, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DNA accessibility is thought to impact the degree to which Oct4 and Sox2 are able to find their target binding sites and interact.
source: DNA accessibility is thought to impact the degree to which Oct4 and Sox2 are able to find their target binding sites and interact (Lam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.
